questions.stem: What must never be altered when balancing an equation?

options.text: The formulae of the reactants and products
options.explanation: Formulae are fixed; only the coefficients in front of them may change.

options.text: The coefficients in front of each formula
options.explanation: Coefficients are precisely what gets adjusted.

options.text: The number of atoms on each side
options.explanation: Equal atom counts are the goal of balancing.
The arrow stays, but that is not what balancing adjusts.

questions.stem: In the balanced equation 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO, what does the coefficient 2 in front of MgO tell you?

options.explanation: Coefficients count formula units, not grams.

options.text: Two formula units of magnesium oxide form per reacting unit of the equation
options.explanation: The coefficient counts formula units; with the other coefficients it fixes the mole ratios 2:1:2.

options.text: Magnesium oxide contains two atoms of magnesium
options.explanation: The subscript, not the coefficient, counts atoms inside a formula.

options.text: The reaction happens twice as fast
options.explanation: Coefficients carry no rate information.

questions.stem: Which state symbol marks a substance dissolved in water?

options.explanation: (g) marks a gas.
(s) marks a solid.
Aqueous means dissolved in water.
(l) marks a pure liquid, not a solution.

questions.stem: In combustion of an organic compound, which order of balancing does the convention recommend?

options.explanation: Fixing oxygen first forces endless rework of the others.
Hydrogen first is workable but not the convention taught.

options.text: Any order, since the result is identical
options.explanation: Any order reaches the same coefficients, but the taught convention keeps working tidy.
The standard routine settles C and H first and lets oxygen absorb the final totals.

questions.stem: A student writes Mg + O2 -> MgO as 'balanced' after writing O as O2 inside the product. What is wrong?

options.text: The product formula was changed; oxygen's diatomic formula was broken to fit the balance
options.explanation: Balancing must keep MgO intact and adjust coefficients instead.
The atom counts may tally but the species written is no longer magnesium oxide.

options.text: The arrow should be an equals sign
options.explanation: Reaction arrows are standard; the fault is the altered formula.
State symbols come last; the fault is deeper.

questions.stem: State the four state symbols and what each denotes.
questions.modelAnswer: (s) denotes solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas and (aq) a substance dissolved in water as an aqueous solution.

questions.stem: List the four steps for writing a balanced equation with state symbols.
questions.modelAnswer: Write the formulae of reactants and products, count the atoms of each element on both sides, balance the atoms one at a time with coefficients, then add the appropriate state symbols.

questions.stem: Explain why changing a product's formula to force a balance is always wrong, even when the atom counts then agree.
questions.modelAnswer: The formula identifies which substance reacts and forms; altering it describes a different reaction entirely, so a balance achieved by tampering documents chemistry that does not exist, while coefficients scale intact formula units without changing any identity.

questions.stem: Magnesium burns in oxygen to give magnesium oxide. Write the fully balanced equation with state symbols, given Mg and MgO are solids and oxygen is a gas.
questions.modelAnswer: 2Mg (s) + O2 (g) -> 2MgO (s); the coefficient pair 2:2 keeps the 1:1 Mg-to-MgO ratio while supplying one intact O2 molecule.

questions.stem: What is the formula of aluminium sulfate, built from Al3+ and SO42-?

options.explanation: The polyatomic ion needs brackets before its subscript.
Two 3+ ions give +6 and three 2- ions give -6: balanced.
That swaps the subscripts; charges would be +9 and -4.
One of each leaves +3 against -2, unbalanced.

questions.stem: Why does an ionic formula need brackets around a polyatomic ion that carries a subscript greater than 1?

options.text: Brackets show the ion is charged
options.explanation: The charge is shown as a superscript on the ion itself.

options.text: Brackets are only needed for gases
options.explanation: Polyatomic ions appear in every state.

options.text: The subscript must multiply every atom inside the group, not just the last one
options.explanation: Al2(SO4)3 means two aluminium plus three complete sulfate groups; without brackets the 3 would read on the oxygen alone.

options.text: Brackets make the formula look tidy
options.explanation: The brackets carry mathematical meaning.

questions.stem: Which pair of ions combines to give the formula Ca3(PO4)2?

options.explanation: Calcium does not form single-charge ions here.

options.text: Ca2+ and PO4-... wait, that would need six phosphates
options.explanation: That mix never cancels at six.
Phosphate is 3-, not 2-; sulfate is the 2- ion.
Three 2+ ions give +6 and two 3- ions give -6.

questions.stem: Iron(III) oxide contains Fe3+ and O2-. What is its formula?

options.explanation: Two 3+ and three 2- cancel at 6.
The subscripts are swapped relative to the charges.
Charges would run +3 against -6.
Charges would run +6 against -2.

questions.stem: A student writes the formula of sodium sulfate as Na(SO4)2 from Na+ and SO42-. What single correction fixes it?

options.explanation: The formula shows no charges anyway; the ion counts are the issue.

options.text: Drop the subscript to give Na2SO4 - two 1+ ions cancel one 2- ion
options.explanation: Sodium needs a subscript 2 on itself, and the sulfate needs no subscript.

options.text: Add brackets and a 2 on sulfate
options.explanation: Sulfate must stay single; the sodium count is the error.
Sodium is always 1+.

questions.stem: State the rule for assembling an ionic formula from the two ion charges.
questions.modelAnswer: Multiply each ion until the positive and negative charges sum to zero, then write the resulting counts as subscripts, bracketing polyatomic ions.

questions.stem: Recall the charges of the sulfate, nitrate, hydroxide and ammonium ions.
questions.modelAnswer: Sulfate is 2-, nitrate is 1-, hydroxide is 1- and ammonium is 1+, so sulfate is the only one of the four carrying a double negative charge.

questions.stem: Explain why swapping the two charge numbers gives the same subscripts as the lowest-common-multiple method.
questions.modelAnswer: If the charges are m+ and n-, the LCM of m and n is m x n for a coprime pair, and dividing by each charge gives n copies of the m+ ion and m copies of the n- ion - exactly the swapped numbers, as in charges 3 and 2 giving Al2(SO4)3.

questions.stem: Write the formula of calcium hydroxide, formed from Ca2+ and OH-, and state the charge balance explicitly.
questions.modelAnswer: Ca(OH)2: one Ca2+ supplies +2 and two OH- ions supply -2, so the charges cancel to zero with brackets preserving the hydroxide group.

questions.stem: What is a spectator ion?

options.text: An ion that makes the solution neutral
options.explanation: Neutrality is a bulk property, not the spectator criterion.

options.text: A solid that precipitates out of solution
options.explanation: The precipitate is usually the product, the opposite of a spectator.

options.text: An ion present in the mixture that takes no part in the reaction
options.explanation: Spectators appear unchanged on both sides and cancel in the ionic equation.

options.text: An ion that changes oxidation state during the reaction
options.explanation: Ions that react change state; spectators do not.

questions.stem: Which species are cancelled when Zn (s) + CuSO4 (aq) -> ZnSO4 (aq) + Cu (s) is converted to an ionic equation?

options.explanation: Zinc is a solid metal that reacts.
Copper is the deposited product.
The sulfate appears on both sides, so cancellation applies.
Sulfate sits dissolved on both sides unchanged.

questions.stem: Which is the correct ionic equation for the zinc and copper(II) sulfate reaction?

options.explanation: Zinc atoms transfer two electrons to copper ions; sulfate is the spectator.
That runs the reaction backwards.
Sulfate is the spectator, not the reactant.
Charges and species are mismatched on both sides.

questions.stem: In an ionic equation, which particles may appear unsplit?

options.text: Only charged species may appear at all
options.explanation: Neutral atoms like Zn (s) and Cu (s) belong in the equation.

options.text: Solids, liquids and gases - only aqueous species dissociate into ions
options.explanation: Dissociation applies to dissolved ionic compounds; intact phases stay whole.

options.text: Every species must be split into ions
options.explanation: Metals and gases carry no ions to split.

options.text: Only the products may stay whole
options.explanation: Splitting depends on state, not on which side the species sits.

questions.stem: Why must charge balance as strictly as atom counts in an ionic equation?

options.text: Because examiners deduct style marks otherwise
options.explanation: The requirement is physical conservation, not presentation.

options.text: It does not - atoms alone must balance
options.explanation: An unbalanced charge would violate electron conservation.

options.text: Charge is conserved: electrons lost by one species are gained by another
options.explanation: The electron transfer leaves the total charge unchanged from side to side.

options.text: Charge balance only matters for precipitation reactions
options.explanation: Every ionic equation obeys charge conservation.

questions.stem: State what happens to ionic compounds when they dissolve in aqueous solution.
questions.modelAnswer: Aqueous ionic compounds dissociate into their separate positive and negative ions, which move freely through the solution.

questions.stem: Outline how to derive an ionic equation from a full balanced equation.
questions.modelAnswer: Split the aqueous compounds into their ions, keep solids, liquids and gases intact, then cancel the spectator ions that appear unchanged on both sides.

questions.stem: Explain why the sulfate ion is a spectator in the zinc and copper(II) sulfate reaction.
questions.modelAnswer: The sulfate ion exists dissolved before the reaction and remains dissolved after zinc has displaced copper, appearing identically on both sides, so it transfers no electrons and takes no part in the chemical change.

questions.stem: Bromine water displaces iodine from potassium iodide: Br2 + 2KI -> I2 + 2KBr. Write the ionic equation and name the spectator.
questions.modelAnswer: Br2 (aq) + 2I- (aq) -> I2 (aq) + 2Br- (aq); the potassium ion is the spectator that cancels from both sides.

questions.stem: Br2 (aq) + 2KI (aq) -> I2 (aq) + 2KBr (aq): which reaction does this displacement equation show?

options.explanation: Salt formation alone does not make a neutralisation; an acid and base must react.
Colour change here is iodine in solution, not a solid precipitate.

options.text: Combustion, because bromine is an oxidant
options.explanation: No oxide forms; the pattern is displacement.

options.text: Displacement, because bromine takes iodide's place
options.explanation: The more reactive halogen displaces the less reactive one from its salt.

questions.stem: Which ionic equation is the signature of an acid-base neutralisation?

options.explanation: The proton meets the hydroxide to form water.
That is the carbonate variant, which additionally releases carbon dioxide.
That is a precipitation signature.
That is metal displacement.

questions.stem: BaCl2 (aq) + Na2SO4 (aq) -> BaSO4 (s) + 2NaCl (aq) shows which observation?

options.text: The solutions simply mixing with no change
options.explanation: The insoluble product is the whole point.

options.text: A white solid forming as barium sulfate settles out
options.explanation: Two clear solutions react to give an insoluble white precipitate.
No gas is produced in this equation.

options.text: A solution changing from blue to colourless
options.explanation: No coloured species participates here.

questions.stem: Why does aqueous bromine demand a fume cupboard and nitrile gloves in a displacement experiment?

options.text: Because the reaction releases hydrogen gas
options.explanation: No hydrogen forms in halogen displacement.

options.text: Because all aqueous solutions are corrosive
options.explanation: Hazard depends on the specific reagent and concentration.

options.text: Bromine itself is classified toxic, corrosive and environmentally harmful, and even bromine water is corrosive above 0.2 mol dm^-3
options.explanation: The reagent's hazard profile, read from the equation's species, drives the precautions.
KI is low hazard; the bromine is the risk.

questions.stem: A student adds sodium carbonate to nitric acid and sees bubbling. Which ionic equation explains the gas?

options.explanation: That produces water silently, no bubbles.
Sodium nitrate stays dissolved; nothing bubbles.
Carbonates do not decompose that way in acid.
The carbonate meets protons, releasing carbon dioxide gas.

questions.stem: State the defining observation of a precipitation reaction.
questions.modelAnswer: Two aqueous solutions react and one product is an insoluble solid, seen as a precipitate that clouds or settles from the mixture.

questions.stem: State the ionic equation for the neutralisation of any strong acid by any alkali.
questions.modelAnswer: H+ (aq) + OH- (aq) -> H2O (l); the acid supplies the proton and the alkali supplies the hydroxide.

questions.stem: Explain why the ionic equation is the clearer view of a precipitation reaction than the full equation.
questions.modelAnswer: The full equation lists four dissolved species, but only the barium and sulfate ions actually combine into the insoluble solid; the sodium and chloride ions cancel as spectators, so the ionic equation Ba2+ + SO42- -> BaSO4 shows the chemical change alone.

questions.stem: A planchet of zinc is dropped into copper(II) sulfate solution and a reddish deposit forms. Write the full equation with state symbols and the matching ionic equation, and name the observation each explains.
questions.modelAnswer: Full: Zn (s) + CuSO4 (aq) -> ZnSO4 (aq) + Cu (s); ionic: Zn + Cu2+ -> Zn2+ + Cu; the reddish deposit is the copper product and the blue colour fading tracks the Cu2+ ions being consumed.
